name: Piroctone olamine

lead: Piroctone olamine is an antifungal ingredient in many anti-dandruff shampoos. People use it to clear flakes and itch and keep the scalp healthy, so hair looks cleaner.

It targets the Malassezia yeasts linked to flaking. It is thought to enter fungal cells and bind iron, disrupting energy production, though the exact mechanism is not fully established. Studies have compared it with zinc pyrithione and ketoconazole shampoos for dandruff and shedding; it is a scalp-condition ingredient rather than a hair-growth treatment.

paras: It is used as a regular wash-in shampoo, lathered on the scalp and rinsed, often a few times a week. It is sold under names such as Octopirox in cosmetic formulations. Flaking typically eases over a few weeks of regular use.
EU rules cap it at 1.0% in rinse-off and 0.5% in other cosmetics. Labels advise avoiding the eyes and stopping use if irritation or allergy occurs.

angle.text: Piroctone olamine is an anti-dandruff shampoo ingredient that acts on scalp yeasts, clearing flakes and itch so the scalp and hair look cleaner. Trials have compared it with zinc pyrithione for dandruff; hair growth is not its documented use.

lead: Piroctone olamine is the ethanolamine salt of piroctone, a hydroxypyridone-type antifungal used in anti-dandruff shampoos and scalp-care products and sold as a raw material by Clariant under the name Octopirox.[1][2] People use it to clear the white or grey flakes and itch of dandruff and mild seborrheic dermatitis, so the hair and shoulders look clean and the scalp is calmer and less greasy.[3][4]

It targets Malassezia yeasts, which are associated with dandruff and seborrheic dermatitis.[3][5] Several comparative trials have tested piroctone olamine shampoos against zinc pyrithione shampoos,[6][7] and two randomised placebo-controlled studies reported that piroctone olamine products reduced hair shedding and increased hair amount on phototrichogram in women with self-perceived thinning.[8][9] In the EU it is permitted as a cosmetic ingredient up to 1.0% in rinse-off and 0.5% in other products.[2]

It is an ingredient rather than a hair-growth drug: the hair studies concern shedding and scalp condition, and it is not a replacement for finasteride or minoxidil in androgenetic alopecia, a point consistent with expert guidance that lists other interventions for that condition.[10]
infobox: Cosmetic ingredient in the EU; OTC dandruff active in some US products[6]

paras: The main use is dandruff and mild seborrheic dermatitis of the scalp, in shampoos and conditioners.[1][2] Wikipedia's dandruff article describes dandruff as heavy flaking that can affect self-esteem and social life, lists piroctone olamine among antifungal agents considered effective, and says climbazole and piroctone olamine are common outside the US.[11] Manufacturers also describe a reduction in hair greasiness, and a 2016 study of a sulfate-free shampoo reported that 0.5% piroctone olamine appeared to influence sebum rheology and reduce greasing.[12]
Because the ingredient is mild and leaves colour unchanged, brands position it as an option for coloured or frequently washed hair; Grokipedia reports it does not fade coloured hair.[1]

A US over-the-counter product combines piroctone olamine with salicylic acid for dandruff; its label says it helps prevent recurrence of flaking and itching and advises against use on broken or inflamed scalp, in children under 12, or in pregnancy.[13] Reviews of seborrheic dermatitis describe Malassezia colonisation, sebaceous gland activity and immune and hormonal factors as contributors and list antifungal shampoos among standard topical management.[3][14]

It is generally described as an antifungal that suppresses scalp microorganisms, especially Malassezia species. Proposed mechanisms include penetrating the fungal membrane and chelating iron, which interferes with mitochondrial energy metabolism, or inhibiting ergosterol synthesis; Wikipedia states the exact mechanism has not been fully established.[1][2] Grokipedia describes the effect as mainly cytostatic and reports it is structurally related to ciclopirox olamine.[1]

Dandruff itself is attributed by Wikipedia to a combination of sebum, microbial by-products such as oleic acid released by Malassezia globosa lipase, and individual susceptibility, with fungal levels reported at roughly 1.5 to 2 times normal in affected people.[11]

Studies in International Journal of Cosmetic Science have examined how much piroctone olamine is retained on skin from shampoos and how solvent systems affect delivery, because rinse-off products have limited contact time.[15][16][17]

Piroctone olamine is the monoethanolamine salt of a 1-hydroxy-2-pyridone bearing a methyl and a branched trimethylpentyl group, formula C16H30N2O3, a white to slightly yellowish crystalline powder only slightly soluble in water.[1][2] Wikipedia states that it was first synthesised in 1979 by Schwarzkopf-Henkel in Germany.[2] It was later used in shampoos as an alternative to zinc pyrithione and ketoconazole, and the compounds have been compared in head-to-head studies since the 1990s.[6][7][18]

Comparative work is the core of the literature. A 2011 trial in people with moderate to severe dandruff compared a shampoo with 0.5% piroctone olamine and 0.45% climbazole against a 1% zinc pyrithione shampoo,[6] and a 2000 study compared a piroctone olamine and salicylic acid shampoo with a zinc pyrithione shampoo.[7] A 2002 study compared 1% ketoconazole, 1% piroctone olamine and 1% zinc pyrithione for effects on hair shedding.[18] A 2017 randomised comparative trial looked at Malassezia populations on seborrheic dermatitis scalps before and after treatment.[4] Wikipedia's dandruff article adds that ketoconazole appears to act for longer than other antifungals.[11]
A 2024 randomised trial examined changes in the scalp microbiome with an effective piroctone olamine shampoo.[19]

Regulators in the EU list it in Annex V of the Cosmetics Regulation with the maximum concentrations above.[2] The product label cited above warns of external use only, avoiding eyes and mucous membranes, and stopping use if an allergic reaction or irritation persists.[13] Grokipedia reports that undiluted material can irritate skin, eyes and airways while diluted cosmetic formulations are well tolerated.[1]

Dandruff trials: a 2011 randomised comparison tested a 0.5% piroctone olamine and 0.45% climbazole shampoo against 1% zinc pyrithione in moderate to severe dandruff;[6] a 2000 study compared a piroctone olamine and salicylic acid shampoo with a zinc pyrithione shampoo;[7] a 2017 trial studied Malassezia yeasts on seborrheic dermatitis scalps.[4] A 2016 clinical trial in 41 subjects of a sulfate-free shampoo with 0.5% piroctone olamine reported high anti-dandruff efficacy, reduced Malassezia density and good persistence after washing.[12]

Hair shedding trials: a 2021 eight-week randomised double-blind study in women with self-perceived thinning reported statistically significant increases in hair amount by phototrichogram with piroctone olamine shampoo and leave-on treatment versus placebo, along with lower oxidative stress and better scalp condition for the shampoo.[9] A 24-week randomised double-blind placebo-controlled study of a regimen combining piroctone olamine, zinc pyrithione, zinc carbonate, niacinamide, panthenol and caffeine reported significant effects on shedding and scalp condition.[8] A 2002 comparative study examined shedding with ketoconazole, piroctone olamine and zinc pyrithione shampoos.[18]

Registered studies include a completed 2025 trial of routine versus shampoo-only care over four weeks with twelve weeks of follow-up in 80 people with dandruff (NCT07133334) and a completed 2026 phase 4 study of a 0.75% piroctone olamine shampoo on scalp microbiota in women with seborrheic dermatitis (NCT07802808).[20][21] A randomised study of a cream containing piroctone olamine among other agents with benzoyl peroxide has also been reported in acne.[22]

Piroctone olamine appears on ingredient lists as piroctone olamine or Octopirox and is a staple of European anti-dandruff shampoo lines. It is a scalp-health ingredient that people pair with their hair routine; forum discussion of it is sparse compared with discussion of hair-growth drugs.
